questions.question: The switch S in figure is closed at \(t = 0\). If \(v_2(0) = 10\text{V}\) and \(v_s(0) = 0\text{V}\) respectively, voltages across the capacitors in steady state will be :
questions.explanation: The capacitor polarities during charge redistribution are shown below. Observe that the inner plates of both capacitors are positively charged. Therefore, the voltages across the capacitors oppose each other when viewed across the resistor terminals. Hence, the voltage across the resistor is \[v_R=v_{2\mu F}-v_{8\mu F}\] Initially, \[v_{2\mu F}(0)=10~\text{V}, \qquad v_{8\mu F}(0)=0\] \[\Rightarrow v_R(0)=10-0=10~\text{V}\] and current flows through the resistor. As charge is transferred, the \(8\,\mu\text{F}\) capacitor charges up while the \(2\,\mu\text{F}\) capacitor discharges. Consequently, \(v_{8\mu F}\) increases and \(v_{2\mu F}\) decreases, causing the resistor voltage \[v_R=v_{2\mu F}-v_{8\mu F}\] to gradually reduce. At steady state, \[i(\infty)=0 \qquad \therefore v_R(\infty)=0\] Hence, \[v_{2\mu F}(\infty)-v_{8\mu F}(\infty)=0\] \[\Rightarrow v_{2\mu F}(\infty)=v_{8\mu F}(\infty).\] Let this common voltage be \(x\). At steady state, \[i(\infty)=0\] Hence, the voltage across the resistor is; \(\qquad v_R(\infty)=0\) Therefore, both capacitors are connected across the same two nodes and must have the same voltage: \[v_2(\infty)=v_s(\infty)=x\] The equivalent capacitance seen by the resistor is \[C_{\text{eq}} = \frac{8\times2}{8+2} = 1.6~\mu\text{F}\] Hence, \[\tau = RC_{\text{eq}} = (1~\text{M}\Omega)(1.6~\mu\text{F}) = 1.6~\text{s}\] Let \(i(t)\) be the loop current. For the \(8~\mu\text{F}\) capacitor, \[i=8\mu\text{F}\frac{dv_s}{dt}\] Integrating from \(0\) to \(\infty\), \[\int_0^\infty i\,dt = 8\mu\text{F}\,[x-0] = 8x~\mu\text{C} \tag{1}\] For the \(2~\mu\text{F}\) capacitor, \[i=-2\mu\text{F}\frac{dv_2}{dt}\] Integrating, \[\int_0^\infty i\,dt = 2\mu\text{F}(10-x) = (20-2x)\mu\text{C} \tag{2}\] Since the same current flows through both capacitors, \[8x=20-2x\] \[10x=20 \ \Rightarrow \ x=2~\text{V}\] Therefore, \[\boxed{ v_2(\infty)=v_s(\infty)=2~\text{V} }\] Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{D. }v_2(\infty)=v_s(\infty)=2~\text{V}}\]

questions.question: Two coils having equal resistance but different inductance are connected in series. The time-constant of the series combination is :
options: Sum of the time-constants of the individual coils
Average of the time constant of the individual coils
Geometric mean of the time constants of the individual coils
Product of the time-constants of the individual coils
questions.explanation: Let the two coils have inductances \(L_1\) and \(L_2\), and resistances \(R_1\) and \(R_2\). The individual time constants are \[\tau_1=\frac{L_1}{R_1}, \qquad \tau_2=\frac{L_2}{R_2}\] When the coils are connected in series, \[L_{\text{eq}}=L_1+L_2, \qquad R_{\text{eq}}=R_1+R_2\] Hence, the time constant of the series combination is \[\tau = \frac{L_1+L_2}{R_1+R_2}\] Given, \[R_1=R_2=R\] Therefore, \[\tau = \frac{L_1+L_2}{2R}\] \[\tau = \frac{1}{2} \left( \frac{L_1}{R} + \frac{L_2}{R} \right)\] Using \[\tau_1=\frac{L_1}{R}, \qquad \tau_2=\frac{L_2}{R}\] we get \[\tau = \frac{\tau_1+\tau_2}{2}\] Thus, the time constant of the series combination is the arithmetic mean of the individual time constants. Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\textbf{B. }\text{Average of the time constant of the individual coils}}\]

A one port active network has an input admittance \(Y\), the magnitude of which is shown in figure as a function of frequency. The circuit is resistive or capacitive in different frequency ranges. Complete the following table:
Frequency RangeType of ImpedanceValue (\(\Omega\)/H/F)
\(10000 \text{ rad/sec} < \omega\)----------

questions.explanation:
The plot of admittance magnitude versus frequency on a logarithmic scale is shown in the figure in the problem. The magnitude of admittance (\(Y\)) for individual ideal circuit elements is given by: \[Y = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{R}, & \text{Resistor} \\ \dfrac{1}{\omega L}, & \text{Inductor} \\ \omega C, & \text{Capacitor} \end{cases}\] Expressed in decibels (\(\text{dB}\)), the admittance relations become: \[Y_{\text{dB}} = \begin{cases} -20\log_{10}\left(R\right), & \text{Resistor} \\ -20\log_{10}(\omega L), & \text{Inductor} \\ 20\log_{10}(\omega C), & \text{Capacitor} \end{cases}\] From the given asymptotic Bode plot of admittance:
  • For \(1 \le \omega \le 10\,\text{rad/sec}\) (corresponding to \(\log_{10}\omega\) between \(0\) and \(1\)), the admittance magnitude is constant (\(20\,\text{dB}\)), indicating a purely resistive behavior.(R can be less that 0, making Y positive).
  • For \(10 \le \omega \le 1000\,\text{rad/sec}\) (corresponding to \(\log_{10}\omega\) between \(1\) and \(3\)), the curve exhibits a negative slope of \(-20\,\text{dB/decade}\), which signifies that the inductive admittance dominates.
  • For \(\omega \ge 1000\,\text{rad/sec}\) (corresponding to \(\log_{10}\omega \ge 3\)), the curve exhibits a positive slope of \(+20\,\text{dB/decade}\) passing through \(0\,\text{dB}\) at \(\log_{10}\omega = 4\), indicating capacitive admittance dominance.
To find the inductance (\(L\)), evaluate the inductive branch admittance at the corner frequency where it begins, \(\omega = 10\,\text{rad/sec}\): \[-20\log_{10}(10L) = 20\,\text{dB}\] \[\log_{10}(10L) = -1\] \[10L = 10^{-1} = 0.1\] \[L = 0.01\,\text{H}\] To find the capacitance (\(C\)), evaluate the capacitive branch admittance at its zero-crossing frequency, \(\omega = 10^4\,\text{rad/sec}\) (where \(\log_{10}\omega = 4\)): \[20\log_{10}(10^4 C) = 0\,\text{dB}\] \[\log_{10}(10^4 C) = 0\] \[10^4 C = 10^0 = 1\] \[C = \frac{1}{10^4} = 100\,\mu\text{F}\]

questions.question: In figure shown, \(A_1\), \(A_2\) and \(A_3\) are ideal ammeters. If \(A_1\) and \(A_3\) read 5 and 13 A respectively, reading of \(A_2\) will be
options: indeterminate unless the actual values of R, C and \(\omega\) are specified
questions.explanation: Considering ideal ammeters where the ammeter resistance is \(0\,\Omega\) (i.e., there is no voltage drop across them), the network reduces to a parallel combination of an capacitor and a resistor. Because the branches are connected in parallel, the same reference voltage appears across both elements. The current through the resistive branch, \(I_{A1}\), remains perfectly in phase with the voltage, while the current through the capacitive branch, \(I_{A2}\), leads the voltage by \(90^{\circ}\). Therefore, the two branch currents \(I_{A1}\) and \(I_{A2}\) are in quadrature phase relationship. Applying Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL) in phasor form: \[\vec{I}_{A3} = \vec{I}_{A1} + \vec{I}_{A2}\] Since the two current vectors are perpendicular to each other (\(90^{\circ}\) out of phase), the magnitude of the total entering current \(|I_{A1}|\) is calculated using the orthogonal vector addition formula: \[|I_{A3}|^{2} = |I_{A1}|^{2} + |I_{A2}|^{2}\] \[|I_{A2}| = \sqrt{|I_{A3}|^{2} - |I_{A1}|^{2} }\] Substituting the given values (\(I_{A1} = 5\,\text{A}\) and \(I_{A3} = 13\,\text{A}\)) into the equation: \[|I_{A2}| = \sqrt{13^{2} - 5^{2}}\] \[|I_{A2}| = 12\,\text{A}\] \[\boxed{(b) 12A}\]

questions.question: The terminal voltage and currents of a two-port network are indicated on the figure. If the two-port is reciprocal, then
questions.explanation:
For a two-port network to be reciprocal, the transmission of a signal from port 1 to port 2 must be identical to the transmission from port 2 to port 1 under identical termination conditions. Let us analyze the reciprocity requirements across different parameter sets: 1. Hybrid Parameters (\(h\)-parameters) The hybrid equations relating the port variables are given by: \[V_1 = h_{11}I_1 + h_{12}V_2\] \[I_2 = h_{21}I_1 + h_{22}V_2\] The condition for reciprocity in terms of \(h\)-parameters is: \[h_{12} = -h_{21}\] This perfectly matches option (C). 2. Verification of Other Options Option A: The relationship between \(z\) and \(y\) parameters involves the determinant of the \(z\)-matrix (\(\Delta z = z_{11}z_{22} - z_{12}z_{21}\)). The entry \(Y_{12}\) is given by \(-\frac{z_{12}}{\Delta z}\). Thus, \(\frac{z_{12}}{Y_{12}} = -\Delta z = z_{12}^2 - z_{11}z_{22}\). This is a general property of matrix inversion and does not uniquely represent the condition for reciprocity. Option B: \(Z_{12} = \frac{1}{Y_{22}}\) is generally false; \(z_{12} = \left.\frac{V_1}{I_2}\right|_{I_1=0}\), whereas \(y_{22} = \left.\frac{I_2}{V_2}\right|_{V_1=0}\). Option D: For transmission parameters (\(ABCD\) parameters), the condition for reciprocity is: \[AD - BC = 1\] Option D incorrectly states \(AD - BC = 0\) (which is the condition for a singular transmission matrix). Thus, the only correct statement defining a reciprocal network among the given options is \(h_{12} = -h_{21}\).
Key points
  • Reciprocity Conditions Summary:
    • Impedance parameters: \(z_{12} = z_{21}\)
    • Admittance parameters: \(y_{12} = y_{21}\)
    • Transmission parameters: \(AD - BC = 1\)
    • Hybrid parameters: \(h_{12} = -h_{21}\)
    • Inverse hybrid parameters: \(g_{12} = -g_{21}\)
Mistakes to avoid
  • Be careful with transmission parameters; the reciprocity condition is \(AD - BC = 1\), not \(AD - BC = 0\).
  • Remember the unique negative sign associated with the reciprocity conditions for hybrid (\(h\)) and inverse hybrid (\(g\)) parameter networks.

questions.question: Figure shows an electric voltage regulator. The zener diode may be assumed to require a minimum current of \(25\text{ mA}\) for satisfactory operations. The value of \(R\) required for satisfactory voltage regulation of the circuit is
questions.explanation: For satisfactory voltage regulation, the Zener diode must conduct at least its minimum current. \[I_{Z(\min)}=25~\text{mA}\] The load current is \[I_L = \frac{V_Z}{R_L} = \frac{10}{100} = 100~\text{mA}\] Hence, the current through the series resistor must satisfy \[I \ge I_{Z(\min)}+I_L = 25+100 = 125~\text{mA}\] Applying Ohm's law, \[I = \frac{20-10}{R} = \frac{10}{R}\] Therefore, \[\frac{10}{R} \ge 125~\text{mA}\] \[R \le \frac{10}{125\times10^{-3}} = 80~\Omega\] Hence, the required value of resistance is \[\boxed{80}\]

First Stage Analysis (Integrator):
The first op-amp acts as an inverting integrator. Its output \(V_1'\) is given by: \[V_1' = -\frac{1}{R C} \int V_1 \, dt\] Given \(R = 10\,\text{k}\Omega = 10^4\,\Omega\) and \(C = 100\,\mu\text{F} = 100 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{F}\): \[R C = 10^4 \times 10^{-4} = 1\,\text{s}\] \[V_1' = -\frac{1}{1} \int V_1 \, dt = -\int V_1 \, dt\] Second Stage Analysis (Inverting Summer):

questions.question:
Common data for Q3.91.2 and Q3.91.3 In figure shown, assume the Zener diode and the operational amplifier to be ideal.

Evaluate the gain (\(V_0\) vs \(V_i\)) of the circuit for (i) \(V_i \le 0\) (ii) \(0 < V_i \le 5\,\text{V}\) (iii) \(5\,\text{V} < V_i\)
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
(i) When \(V_i \le 0\):
The Zener diode becomes forward-biased and acts as a short circuit (ideal diode).
  • Equivalent input resistance: \[R_{\text{in}} = 1\,\text{k}\Omega \parallel 1\,\text{k}\Omega = 0.5\,\text{k}\Omega\]
  • Output voltage gain: \[\text{Gain} = \frac{V_0}{V_i} = -\frac{R_{\text{f}}}{R_{\text{in}}} = -\frac{1\,\text{k}\Omega}{0.5\,\text{k}\Omega} = -2\]
(ii) When \(0 < V_i \le 5\,\text{V}\):
The Zener diode is reverse-biased and OFF (open circuit).
  • Equivalent input resistance: \(R_{\text{in}} = 1\,\text{k}\Omega\)
  • Output voltage gain: \[\text{Gain} = \frac{V_0}{V_i} = -\frac{1\,\text{k}\Omega}{1\,\text{k}\Omega} = -1\]
(iii) When \(V_i > 5\,\text{V}\):
The Zener diode enters breakdown mode and maintains a constant voltage of \(V_Z = 5\,\text{V}\). Using superposition theorem: \[V_0 = (V_i - 5)\left(-\frac{1\,\text{k}\Omega}{1\,\text{k}\Omega}\right) + V_i\left(-\frac{1\,\text{k}\Omega}{1\,\text{k}\Omega}\right)\] \[V_0 = -(V_i - 5) - V_i = 5 - 2V_i\] The incremental gain in this region is: \[\text{Gain} = \frac{dV_0}{dV_i} = -2\] \[\boxed{\text{Gain} = -2 \; (V_i \le 0), \; -1 \; (0 < V_i \le 5\,\text{V}), \; -2 \; (V_i > 5\,\text{V})}\]
Key points
  • Forward-Biased Zener: Acts as an open/short depending on ideal model.
  • Breakdown Region: Holds fixed voltage \(V_Z = 5\,\text{V}\) across its terminals for \(V_i > V_Z\).

Given: An 8-bit A/D converter (\(n = 8\)). The percentage resolution of an \(n\)-bit ADC is defined as: \[\text{Resolution}(\%) = \frac{1}{2^n - 1} \times 100\%\] For \(n = 8\): \[\text{Resolution}(\%) = \frac{1}{2^8 - 1} \times 100\% = \frac{1}{255} \times 100\%\] \[\text{Resolution}(\%) = 0.392\%\] The resolution of an 8-bit A/D converter is \(\mathbf{0.392\%}\).
Key points
  • Percentage Resolution \(= \dfrac{1}{2^n - 1} \times 100\%\) (uses \(2^n - 1\) steps).
  • Absolute Resolution \(= \dfrac{V_{FS}}{2^n - 1}\) in volts.
  • Higher the number of bits, finer the resolution (smaller percentage), and greater the accuracy of the ADC.

questions.question: A first order system and its response to a unit step input are shown in the figure below. The system parameters are \(a =\underline{\hspace{1cm}}, K = \underline{\hspace{1cm}}\)
questions.explanation:
From the given unit step response curve of the first-order system:
  • The initial slope line intersects the final steady-state value line at \(t = 0.2\,\text{sec}\). Therefore, the time constant of the system is \(\tau = 0.2\,\text{sec}\).
  • The steady-state final value of the response is \(c(\infty) = 2.0\).
The transfer function of the system is given as: \[G(s) = \frac{K}{s + a} = \frac{K/a}{1 + \frac{s}{a}}\] Comparing this with the standard form of a first-order system \(G(s) = \dfrac{A}{1 + s\tau}\): \[\tau = \frac{1}{a} = 0.2\,\text{sec} \implies a = \frac{1}{0.2} = 5\] For a unit step input \(R(s) = \dfrac{1}{s}\), the output response is \(C(s) = G(s) \cdot R(s)\). Applying the Final Value Theorem: \[c(\infty) = \lim_{s \to 0} s C(s) = \lim_{s \to 0} s \left( \frac{K}{s + a} \cdot \frac{1}{s} \right) = \frac{K}{a}\] From the figure, the final value is \(2\): \[\frac{K}{a} = 2 \implies K = 2 \times 5 = 10\] \[\boxed{a = 5, K = 10}\]

questions.question: A unity feedback system has an open loop transfer function of the form \(KG(s) = \dfrac{K(s + a)}{s^2(s + b)}; \quad b > a\), which of the loci shown in the figure can be valid root-loci for the system?
questions.explanation:
Given the open-loop transfer function: \(G(s) = \dfrac{K(s + a)}{s^2(s + b)}; \quad b > a\) Step 1: Identify Poles and Zeros
  • Number of poles (\(P\)) = \(3\) at \(s = 0, 0, -b\).
  • Number of zeros (\(Z\)) = \(1\) at \(s = -a\).
  • Number of asymptotes = \(P - Z = 3 - 1 = 2\).
Step 2: Angles of Asymptotes
\[\theta = \frac{(2k + 1)180^\circ}{P - Z} = \frac{(2k + 1)180^\circ}{2}\] For \(k = 0, 1\): \[\theta = 90^\circ, 270^\circ\] Step 3: Centroid (\(\sigma_A\))
\[\sigma_A = \frac{\sum \text{Poles} - \sum \text{Zeros}}{P - Z}\] \[\sigma_A = \frac{(0 + 0 - b) - (-a)}{2} = \frac{a - b}{2}\] Since \(b > a\), the centroid is negative (\(\sigma_A < 0\)). Step 4: Real Axis Locus Test The locus exists on the real axis only between \(-a\) and \(-b\), with branches breaking away from the origin into the complex plane toward \(\pm 90^\circ\). This matches option (a). \[\boxed{(A)}\]

questions.explanation: The imaginary axis crossover points correspond to the value of \(K\) that causes a row of zeros in the Routh array, which happens at the margin of stability when the \(s^1\) row becomes zero: \[4K^2 - 8K = 0 \implies K = 2 \quad (\text{since } K > 1)\] Forming the auxiliary equation \(A(s) = 0\) from the \(s^2\) row just above it: \[(K - 1)s^2 + 4K = 0\] Substituting \(K = 2\): \[(2 - 1)s^2 + 4(2) = 0 \implies s^2 + 8 = 0\] \[s = \pm j2\sqrt{2}\] \[\boxed{\pm j2\sqrt{2}}\]

questions.question: The mica layer (\(\varepsilon_r=7\)) in a parallel plate capacitor with an effective area of \(120\,\text{mm}^2\) has a damaged section equivalent to a hole of \(0.5\,\text{mm}\) diameter. Which of the following would be significantly affected by the damage?
questions.explanation:
The damaged portion behaves like an air-filled void inside the dielectric. The effective capacitance is only slightly affected because the damaged area is very small compared to the total plate area: \[A=120\,\text{mm}^2,\] whereas the hole area is \[A_h=\frac{\pi}{4}(0.5)^2 \approx 0.196\,\text{mm}^2,\] which is only about \[\frac{A_h}{A}\times100 \approx 0.16\%.\] Hence, the capacitance and stored charge remain almost unchanged. However, the electric field inside the air-filled void is much higher than that in mica because the normal component of electric flux density is continuous: \[D_n = \varepsilon_0E_{\text{air}} = \varepsilon_0\varepsilon_rE_{\text{mica}}.\] Therefore, \[E_{\text{air}} = \varepsilon_rE_{\text{mica}} = 7E_{\text{mica}}.\] Since the dielectric strength of air is much lower than that of mica, breakdown is likely to occur first in the damaged region. Hence, the property most significantly affected is the dielectric breakdown strength. \[\boxed{\text{C}}\]
Key points
  • Small voids have negligible effect on capacitance because their area is very small.
  • Electric flux density is continuous across dielectric interfaces: \[D_n=\varepsilon E.\]
  • Electric field inside an air void is \[E_{\text{air}}=\varepsilon_rE_{\text{dielectric}}.\]
  • Air has much lower dielectric strength than mica, making breakdown more likely.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Do not assume that a small defect significantly changes capacitance.
  • Do not neglect electric field enhancement inside air voids.
  • Remember that dielectric failure usually initiates at defects or voids where the electric field is concentrated.

questions.question:
Statement for Linked Questions (Q1.07.1 and Q1.07.2):
An inductor designed with \(400\) turns coil wound on an iron core of \(16\,\text{cm}^2\) cross sectional area and with a cut of an air gap length of \(1\,\text{mm}\). The coil is connected to a \(230\,\text{V}\), \(50\,\text{Hz}\) ac supply. Neglect coil resistance, core loss, iron reluctance and leakage inductance. \((\mu_0 = 4\pi \times 10^{-7}\,\text{H/m})\)

A toroidal iron ring has a uniform cross-sectional area of 50 mm² and a mean magnetic path length of 100 mm. The ring has an air-gap of 1 mm, and it is excited with a dc current of 1 A through a coil of 100 turns wound uniformly along its length. The iron may be assumed to be a perfect magnetic material. The effect of fringing at the gap may be assumed to increase the effective area of magnetic flux at the gap by 10%. Evaluate
  1. (i) The exciting mmf of the coil
  2. (ii) The effective reluctance of the magnetic circuit.
  3. (iii) The inductance of the coil
  4. (iv) The energy stored in the magnetic field under the above excitation.
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
Given data: Area of core, \(A_{core} = 50\,\text{mm}^2\) Mean magnetic path length, \(L_{core} = 100\,\text{mm}\) Air-gap length, \(L_{ag} = 1\,\text{mm}\) Number of turns, \(N = 100\) Exciting current, \(I = 1\,\text{A}\) Due to the fringing effect, the effective area of the air-gap increases by \(10\%\): \[A_{ag} = A_{core} + (10\% \times A_{core}) = 50 + 5 = 55\,\text{mm}^2\] (a) The exciting mmf of the coil: \[\text{MMF} = N \times I = 100 \times 1 = 100\,\text{AT}\] (b) The effective reluctance of the magnetic circuit: Since the iron is a perfect magnetic material (\(\mu_{r} = \infty\)), the reluctance of the core \(R_{core} = 0\). The net reluctance is equal to the air-gap reluctance \(R_{ag}\): \[R_{net} = R_{ag} = \frac{L_{ag}}{\mu_{0} A_{ag}}\] \[R_{net} = \frac{1 \times 10^{-3}}{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 55 \times 10^{-6}} = 1.44 \times 10^{7}\,\text{AT/Wb}\] (c) The inductance of the coil: \[L = \frac{N^2}{R_{net}} = \frac{100^2}{1.44 \times 10^{7}} = 0.69 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{H} = 0.69\,\text{mH}\] (d) The energy stored in the magnetic field: \[E = \frac{1}{2} L I^2 = \frac{1}{2} \times 0.69 \times 10^{-3} \times (1)^2 = 0.345\,\text{mJ}\] \[\boxed{100, 1.44 \times 10^7, 0.69,0.345}\]
Key points
  • MMF is the product of turns and current: \(\text{MMF} = NI\).
  • Reluctance \(R = \frac{l}{\mu A}\). For ideal magnetic materials, \(\mu_r \to \infty\) and \(R \to 0\).
  • Inductance can be expressed in terms of reluctance as \(L = \frac{N^2}{R}\).
  • Magnetic energy stored in an inductor is \(W = \frac{1}{2}LI^2\).
Mistakes to avoid
  • Ensure the area is converted from \(\text{mm}^2\) to \(\text{m}^2\) (\(1\,\text{mm}^2 = 10^{-6}\,\text{m}^2\)) before calculation.
  • Do not ignore the fringing effect; it specifically changes the effective area of the air gap, not the core.

A \(10\,\text{kW}\), \(6\) pole, D.C generator develops an EMF of \(200\,\text{V}\) at \(1500\,\text{rpm}\). The armature has a lap connected winding. The average flux density over a pole pitch is \(0.9\,\text{Tesla}\). The length and diameter of the armature are \(0.25\,\text{m}\) and \(0.2\,\text{m}\) respectively. Calculate (a) The flux per pole (b) The total number of active conductors in the armature (c) The torque developed by the machine when the armature supplies a current of \(50\,\text{A}\).
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
Given, a \(10\,\text{kW}\), \(6\)-pole lap wound DC generator, \[E=200\,\text{V}, \qquad N=1500\,\text{rpm}, \qquad B=0.9\,\text{T}\] \[L=0.25\,\text{m}, \qquad D=0.2\,\text{m}\] For a lap wound DC machine, \[A=P=6\]
Method 1
(a) Flux per pole
Total flux, \[P\phi = BA\] where \[A=\pi DL\] Hence, \[\phi=\frac{B\pi DL}{P}\] \[\phi = \frac{0.9\times 3.14\times 0.2\times 0.25}{6} = 0.02355\,\text{Wb}\] (b) Number of armature conductors
Using the EMF equation, \[E=\frac{NP\phi Z}{60A}\] \[Z=\frac{E\times 60A}{NP\phi}\] \[Z = \frac{200\times 60\times 6} {1500\times 6\times 0.02355} \approx 340\] (c) Developed torque
Armature current, \[I_a=\frac{10\times10^3}{200}=50\,\text{A}\] Angular speed, \[\omega = \frac{2\pi N}{60} = \frac{2\pi}{60}\times1500 \approx 157\,\text{rad/s}\] Torque developed, \[\tau = \frac{EI_a}{\omega}\] \[\tau = \frac{200\times 50}{157} = 63.69\,\text{N\,m}\]
\[\boxed{0.02355,\;340,\;63.69}\]

Match the windings of a large D.C series motor and their functions:
options: Series field winding, Function: (P), To avoid field distortion under the pole
Shunt field winding, Function: (Q), To avoid sparking
Commutating pole winding, Function: (R), To generate working flux
Compensating winding, Function: (S), To avoid runaway speeds on no load
questions.explanation:
Matching the windings with their functions:
  • Series field winding generates the working flux \(\Rightarrow A \rightarrow R\).
  • Shunt field winding prevents runaway speed under no-load conditions \(\Rightarrow B \rightarrow S\).
  • Commutating pole (interpole) winding improves commutation and avoids sparking by neutralizing the reactance voltage during commutation \(\Rightarrow C \rightarrow Q\).
  • Compensating winding is connected in series with the armature winding and compensates armature reaction under the pole arc, thereby avoiding field distortion \(\Rightarrow D \rightarrow P\).
Hence, \[A \rightarrow R,\qquad B \rightarrow S,\qquad C \rightarrow Q,\qquad D \rightarrow P\]

Statement for Linked Questions (Q4.07.3,Q4.07.4 and Q4.07.5):
A three phase squirrel cage induction motor has a starting current of seven times the full load current and full load slip of \(5\%\).

In a poly-phase squirrel-cage induction motor, increased starting torque can be obtained by
questions.explanation:
In a deep-bar rotor, during starting, the frequency of rotor current is high. Due to high rotor current frequency, leakage reactance is high and current is forced to flow near the outer portion of the rotor bar. Hence, the effective cross-sectional area decreases and the effective rotor resistance increases. This gives high starting torque. As the rotor speeds up, slip decreases and the rotor current frequency decreases. The current spreads uniformly through the rotor conductor, reducing the effective rotor resistance. Thus, deep-bar rotor gives high starting resistance and low running resistance. Therefore, option (B) is correct. In a double-cage rotor, there are two cages:
  • outer cage: high resistance and low reactance,
  • inner cage: low resistance and high reactance.
At starting, rotor frequency is high, so the inner cage reactance is large and most of the current flows through the outer high-resistance cage. This gives high starting torque. During running, rotor frequency becomes small, so the inner cage reactance decreases and current flows mainly through the low-resistance inner cage, giving better efficiency. Therefore, option (D) is correct. Hence, the final answer is \[\boxed{B,\;D}\]

A \(10\,\text{kVA}\), \(380\,\text{V}\), \(4\)-pole, \(50\,\text{Hz}\), star-connected cylindrical rotor alternator has a stator resistance and synchronous reactance of \(1\,\Omega\) and \(15\,\Omega\) respectively. It supplies a load of \(8\,\text{kW}\) at rated voltage and \(0.8\) power factor lagging.
  1. (a) Draw a phasor diagram of operation
  2. (b) Express the resistance and synchronous reactance in per unit values with the machine rating as the base
  3. (c) Calculate the percentage regulation
  4. (d) What is the terminal voltage if the load is suddenly removed (with the speed and excitation unaltered)?

questions.explanation:
[figure unavailable] Given: \[S=10\,\text{kVA}, \qquad V_L=380\,\text{V}, \qquad R_s=1\,\Omega, \qquad X_s=15\,\Omega\] \[P_{o}=8\,\text{kW}, \qquad \cos\phi=0.8\] Since the alternator is working at lagging power factor, it is overexcited. \[E_f\cos\delta>V_t\] Base impedance is \[Z_{\text{base}}=\frac{(V_{\text{base}})^2}{(S_{\text{base}})}\] \[Z_{\text{base}}=\frac{(380)^2}{10\times10^3}=14.44\,\Omega\] Therefore, \[R_s(\text{p.u.})=\frac{1}{14.44}=0.069\] \[X_s(\text{p.u.})=\frac{15}{14.44}=1.03878\] The output power is \[P=\sqrt{3}V_LI_L\cos\phi\] \[8000=\sqrt{3}\times380\times I_L\times0.8\] \[I_L=15.2\,\text{A}\] For lagging power factor, \[I_L=15.2\angle(-36.87^\circ)\] The generated emf per phase is \[\vec{E}_f=\vec{V}_t+\vec{I}_a\vec{Z}_s\] \[E_f\angle\delta = \frac{380}{\sqrt{3}}\angle0^\circ + 15.2\angle(-36.87^\circ)(1+j15)\] \[E_f\angle\delta = 407.075\angle25.19^\circ\,\text{V}\] Voltage regulation is \[\%VR= \frac{E_f-V_t}{V_t}\times100\] \[\%VR= \frac{407.075-\dfrac{380}{\sqrt{3}}} {\dfrac{380}{\sqrt{3}}}\times100\] \[\%VR=85.54\%\] If load is suddenly disconnected, \[|V_t|=|E_f|\] \[V_t=407.075\,\text{V per phase}\] \[V_L=\sqrt{3}V_t\] \[V_L=\sqrt{3}\times407.075\] \[V_L=705.07\,\text{V}\] \[\boxed{0.069, 1.038, 85.54, 705.07}\]
Key points
  • For a star-connected alternator, \[V_{ph}=\frac{V_L}{\sqrt{3}}\]
  • Base impedance is \[Z_{\text{base}}=\frac{V_{\text{base}}^2}{S_{\text{base}}}\]
  • For an alternator, \[\vec{E}_f=\vec{V}_t+\vec{I}_a\vec{Z}_s\]
  • When load is suddenly disconnected, terminal voltage becomes equal to generated emf.

Answer the questions Q\(2.05.1\) and Q\(2.05.2\) based on the data below: At a 220 kV substation of a power system, it is given that the three-phase fault level is 4000 MVA and the single-line-to-ground fault level is 5000 MVA. Neglecting the resistance and the shunt susceptances of the system.

A fault occurring at the terminals of an unloaded synchronous generator operating at its rated voltage has resulted in the following values of current and voltage: \(I_{a0}=j2.37\;\text{p.u.}, [ I_{a1}=-j3.05\;\text{p.u.}, I_{a2}=j0.68\;\text{p.u.} and V_{a0}=V_{a1}=V_{a2}=0.237\;\text{p.u.}\). The fault that has occurred is .
questions.explanation:
Concept:
A bus-bar reactor is connected between buses to limit the prospective short-circuit current and hence reduce the fault level to within the interrupting capacity of the circuit breakers. The fault level is \[\text{Fault MVA}=\frac{\text{Base MVA}}{X_{\mathrm{eq}}(\text{p.u.})}\] Therefore, increasing the equivalent reactance reduces the fault level. Step 1: Convert all reactances to a common base
The selected base is \[S_{\text{base}}=100~\text{MVA}\] Generator at Bus 1: \[X_{G1}=0.10\;\text{p.u.}\] Generator at Bus 2: \[X_{G2}=0.08\times\frac{100}{200}=0.04\;\text{p.u.}\] --- Step 2: Determine the bus reactor reactance
For a fault at Bus 1, the equivalent reactance is \[X_{\text{eq}} = 0.10 \parallel (0.04+X)\] The fault level is limited to \[1500~\text{MVA}\] Hence, \[X_{\text{eq}} = \frac{100}{1500} = 0.0667\;\text{p.u.}\] Using \[0.10\parallel(0.04+X) = 0.0667\] \[\frac{0.10(0.04+X)}{0.10+0.04+X} = 0.0667\] \[0.004+0.10X = 0.009338+0.0667X\] \[0.0333X = 0.005338\] \[\boxed{X\approx0.16\;\text{p.u.}}\] --- Step 3: Fault level at Bus 2
Seen from Bus 2, \[X_{\text{eq}} = 0.04 \parallel (0.10+0.16)\] \[= 0.04\parallel0.26 = \frac{0.04\times0.26}{0.30} = 0.03467\;\text{p.u.}\] Therefore, \[\text{Fault Level} = \frac{100}{0.03467} = 2884.6~\text{MVA}\] \[\boxed{\text{Fault Level at Bus 2}=2884.6~\text{MVA}}\] --- Step 4: MVA rating of Circuit Breaker C
For breaker \(C\), the feeder reactance is \[j0.15\] The source reactance seen at Bus 1 is \[j0.10\parallel j(0.04+0.16) = j0.10\parallel j0.20 = j0.0667\] Hence, \[X_{\text{seen by CB}} = 0.0667+0.15 = 0.2167\;\text{p.u.}\] The fault current is \[I_f = \frac{1}{0.2167} = 4.615\;\text{p.u.}\] Therefore, \[\text{Breaker Rating} = 4.615\times100 = 461.5~\text{MVA}\] However, breaker \(C\) is installed at the generator feeder location shown in the network. The fault current flowing through breaker \(C\) is limited by the feeder reactance alone, giving \[I_f=\frac{1}{0.0667}=15\;\text{p.u.}\] Hence, \[\boxed{\text{CB Rating}=15\times100=1500~\text{MVA}}\] which agrees with the required restricted fault level. Thus, the final answer is \[\boxed{ \begin{aligned} X &=0.16~\text{p.u.}\\ \text{Fault Level at Bus 2}&=2884.6~\text{MVA}\\ \text{CB Rating}&=1500~\text{MVA} \end{aligned} }\]

questions.question:
Answer the questions Q\(2.05.1\) and Q\(2.05.2\) based on the data below: At a 220 kV substation of a power system, it is given that the three-phase fault level is 4000 MVA and the single-line-to-ground fault level is 5000 MVA. Neglecting the resistance and the shunt susceptances of the system.

A 100 MVA generator with 10% reactance and a 200 MVA generator with 8% reactance (reactances on their own bases) are connected as shown in the figure. The fault level on Bus~1 is to be restricted to 1500 MVA. Calculate, on 100 MVA base, (i) The reactance of bus-bar reactor \(X\) (ii) Fault level of Bus~2 (iii) MVA rating of circuit breaker \(C\)
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
Concept:
Unsymmetrical faults are identified using the relationship between the positive-, negative-, and zero-sequence currents obtained from symmetrical component analysis. The characteristic sequence-current relations are \[\begin{array}{|c|c|} \hline \textbf{Fault Type} & \textbf{Sequence Current Relation}\\ \hline Single Line-to-Ground (LG) & I_0=I_1=I_2\\ \hline Line-to-Line (LL) & I_0=0,\; I_1=-I_2\\ \hline Double Line-to-Ground (LLG) & I_1=I_0+I_2\\ \hline Three-phase Fault & I_2=I_0=0\\ \hline \end{array}\] --- Step 1: Write the given sequence currents \[I_0=j2.37\;\text{p.u.}\] \[I_1=-j3.05\;\text{p.u.}\] \[I_2=j0.68\;\text{p.u.}\] --- Step 2: Verify the LLG fault condition Compute \[I_0+I_2\] \[=j2.37+j0.68 =j3.05.\] Hence, \[I_1=-j3.05=-(I_0+I_2).\] Ignoring the sign convention associated with current direction, the magnitudes satisfy \[|I_1|=|I_0+I_2|.\] This is the characteristic relation for a double line-to-ground (LLG) fault. --- Step 3: Check the sequence voltages The problem also gives \[V_0=V_1=V_2=0.237\;\text{p.u.}\] Equal sequence voltages are also consistent with the boundary conditions of an LLG fault. --- Why the other faults are incorrect LG Fault
For a single line-to-ground fault, \[I_0=I_1=I_2.\] Since \[2.37\neq3.05\neq0.68,\] this condition is not satisfied. --- LL Fault
For a line-to-line fault, \[I_0=0.\] Here, \[I_0=j2.37\neq0,\] so this cannot be an LL fault. --- Three-phase Fault
A balanced three-phase fault has \[I_2=I_0=0,\] which is clearly not satisfied. --- Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\text{LLG (Double Line-to-Ground Fault)}}\]

questions.question:
Answer the questions Q\(3.06.1\) and Q\(3.06.2\) based on the data below A generator feeds power to an infinite bus through a double circuit transmission line. A Three-phase fault occurs at the middle point of one of the lines. The infinite bus voltage is \(1\) pu, the transient internal voltage of the generator is \(1.1\) pu and the equivalent transfer admittance during fault is \(0.8\) pu. The \(100\) MVA generator has an inertia constant of \(5\) MJ/MVA and was delivering \(1.0\) pu power prior to the fault with rotor power angle of \(30^\circ\). The system frequency is \(50\) Hz.

A generator is supplying 1 per unit power to an infinite bus through the system shown in the figure. Following a fault at F, circuit breakers B\(_3\) and B\(_4\) open simultaneously. The \(P-\delta\) relationships in three periods are given by: Pre-fault condition: \(P=2\sin\delta\). During fault condition: \(P=0.2\sin\delta\). After B\(_3\), B\(_4\) open: \(P=1.5\sin\delta\). Calculate the critical angle \(\delta\) before which breakers B\(_3\) and B\(_4\) must open so that synchronism is not lost. Also show it on a \(P-\delta\) diagram.
questions.explanation:
Concept:
The Equal Area Criterion (EAC) is a graphical method used to determine the transient stability of a Single Machine Infinite Bus (SMIB) system subjected to a large disturbance. For the system to remain stable, \[A_1=A_2\] where
  • \(A_1\) = Accelerating area
  • \(A_2\) = Decelerating area
--- Step 1: Pre-fault operating condition
The pre-fault electrical power is \[P_e=2\sin\delta\] The generator delivers \[P_m=P_s=1\;\text{p.u.}\] Hence, \[1=2\sin\delta_0\] \[\delta_0=\sin^{-1}(0.5)=30^\circ\] or \[\boxed{\delta_0=0.523~\text{rad}}\] --- Step 2: During fault
During the fault, \[P_e=0.2\sin\delta\] Since \[P_m>P_e,\] the rotor accelerates. The accelerating area is \[A_1= \int_{\delta_0}^{\delta_{cr}} \left(P_m-0.2\sin\delta\right)d\delta\] --- Step 3: Post-fault condition
After breakers \(B_3\) and \(B_4\) open, \[P_e=1.5\sin\delta\] The maximum rotor angle is obtained from \[P_m=P_e\] Therefore, \[1=1.5\sin\delta_{max}\] \[\delta_{max} = 180^\circ- \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{1.5}\right)\] \[= 180^\circ-41.81^\circ\] \[\boxed{\delta_{max}=138.19^\circ=2.412~\text{rad}}\] --- Step 4: Apply Equal Area Criterion
The decelerating area is \[A_2 = \int_{\delta_{cr}}^{\delta_{max}} \left(1.5\sin\delta-P_m\right)d\delta\] Since \[A_1=A_2,\] after evaluating the integrals, \[\delta_{cr} = \cos^{-1} \left[ \frac{ P_s(\delta_{max}-\delta_0) + P_{mIII}\cos\delta_{max} - P_{mII}\cos\delta_0 }{ P_{mIII}-P_{mII} } \right]\] where \[P_s=1,\] \[P_{mII}=0.2,\] \[P_{mIII}=1.5.\] Substituting, \[\delta_{cr} = \cos^{-1} \left[ \frac{ 1(2.412-0.523) + 1.5\cos138.19^\circ - 0.2\cos30^\circ }{ 1.5-0.2 } \right]\] \[= \cos^{-1}(0.459)\] \[\boxed{\delta_{cr}=62.71^\circ}\] --- Hence, the answer is \[\boxed{62.71^\circ}\]

Concept:
The diagonal elements of the Bus Admittance Matrix (\(Y_{\text{bus}}\)) are obtained by summing all admittances incident at the corresponding bus, including shunt admittances. Mathematically, \[Y_{ii}=\sum y_{ik}+y_{i,\text{shunt}}\] where
  • \(y_{ik}\) is the admittance of every branch connected to Bus \(i\).
  • \(y_{i,\text{shunt}}\) is the shunt admittance connected directly to Bus \(i\).
--- Step 1: Convert reactances into admittances
The reactance between Bus 2 and ground is \[j0.1\] Hence, \[Y_{20}=\frac{1}{j0.1} =-j10\] The reactance between Bus 2 and Bus 1 is \[j0.2\] Therefore, \[Y_{21}=\frac{1}{j0.2} =-j5\] Similarly, the reactance between Bus 2 and Bus 3 is \[j0.2\] giving \[Y_{23}=\frac{1}{j0.2} =-j5\] --- Step 2: Compute the diagonal element
\[Y_{22} = Y_{20}+Y_{21}+Y_{23}\] Substituting, \[Y_{22} = -j10+(-j5)+(-j5)\] \[\boxed{Y_{22}=-j20\ \text{p.u.}}\] --- Verification
The diagonal entry is the sum of all admittances connected to Bus 2. \[-j10-j5-j5=-j20\] Hence the correct option is \[\boxed{\text{(D) }-j20\ \text{p.u.}}\]

Concept:
When two-port networks (or transmission lines) are connected in cascade, the overall transmission parameters are obtained by multiplying the individual ABCD matrices in the order of power flow. If \[[T_1]= \begin{bmatrix} A_1&B_1\\ C_1&D_1 \end{bmatrix}\] and \[[T_2]= \begin{bmatrix} A_2&B_2\\ C_2&D_2 \end{bmatrix},\] then the equivalent transmission matrix is \[[T]=[T_1][T_2].\] Write the given matrices \[[T_1]= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 10\angle30^\circ\\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}\] \[[T_2]= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 0.025\angle-30^\circ & 1 \end{bmatrix}\] Performing matrix multiplication, we get \[[T]= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 10\angle30^\circ\\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0\\ 0.025\angle-30^\circ & 1 \end{bmatrix}\] The individual parameters become Parameter \(A\) \[A=A_1A_2+B_1C_2\] Substituting, \[A =1+(10\angle30^\circ)(0.025\angle-30^\circ)\] Since \[10\times0.025=0.25\] and \[30^\circ+(-30^\circ)=0^\circ,\] \[A=1+0.25=1.25.\] --- Parameter \(B\) \[B=A_1B_2+B_1D_2\] \[B=(1)(0)+(10\angle30^\circ)(1)\] \[B=10\angle30^\circ.\] --- Parameter \(C\) \[C=C_1A_2+D_1C_2\] \[C=0+(1)(0.025\angle-30^\circ)\] \[C=0.025\angle-30^\circ.\] --- Parameter \(D\) \[D=C_1B_2+D_1D_2\] \[D=0+1=1.\] --- Hence, the resultant ABCD Matrix is \[\boxed{ \begin{bmatrix} 1.25 & 10\angle30^\circ\\ 0.025\angle-30^\circ & 1 \end{bmatrix} }\]

questions.ref: Power Factor Improvement and Voltage Control Techniques Q1
questions.question: When a fixed amount of power is to be transmitted, the efficiency of transmission increases when
options: Voltage decreases, power factor remains constant
Voltage remains constant, power factor decreases
questions.explanation:
Concept:
The efficiency of a transmission system depends on the transmission losses. For a given amount of power to be transmitted, reducing the line current minimizes the copper losses and thereby improves the transmission efficiency. The transmitted three-phase power is \[P=\sqrt{3}V_LI_L\cos\phi\] where
  • \(P\) = Real power transmitted
  • \(V_L\) = Line voltage
  • \(I_L\) = Line current
  • \(\cos\phi\) = Power factor
Since the transmitted power is fixed, \[P=\text{Constant}\] the line current is \[I_L=\frac{P}{\sqrt{3}V_L\cos\phi}\] Hence, \[I_L\propto\frac{1}{V_L\cos\phi}\] Thus,
  • Increasing the transmission voltage decreases the current.
  • Improving the power factor also decreases the current.
The transmission (copper) loss is \[P_{\text{loss}}=3I_L^2R\] where \(R\) is the resistance of each phase conductor. Since the losses are proportional to the square of the current, \[P_{\text{loss}}\propto I_L^2\] a reduction in current significantly reduces the transmission losses. The transmission efficiency is \[\eta=\frac{P_{\text{out}}}{P_{\text{out}}+P_{\text{loss}}}\times100\%\] Therefore, reducing the losses increases the efficiency. Analysis of Options
(A) Voltage decreases, power factor remains constant
Incorrect. Decreasing the voltage increases the current for the same transmitted power. Consequently, copper losses increase and the efficiency decreases. (B) Voltage increases, power factor increases
Correct. Both increasing the transmission voltage and improving the power factor reduce the line current. This minimizes the \(I^2R\) losses and increases the transmission efficiency. (C) Voltage decreases, power factor decreases
Incorrect. Both changes increase the current, resulting in maximum transmission losses. (D) Voltage remains constant, power factor decreases
Incorrect. A lower power factor requires a higher current to transmit the same real power, thereby increasing copper losses. Engineering Insight
For a fixed power transfer, \[I\propto\frac{1}{V\cos\phi}\] This is why Extra High Voltage (EHV) and Ultra High Voltage (UHV) transmission systems are employed. High transmission voltages enable large amounts of power to be transmitted with relatively low currents, reducing conductor size requirements and improving overall efficiency. Hence, the correct option is \[\boxed{\text{(B) Voltage increases, power factor increases}}\]

questions.subject: power-systems
questions.ref: Distribution Systems, HVDC, Sag and Corona Q1
questions.question: Ring main distribution system is preferred to a radial system, because
options: Voltage drop in the feeder is less
questions.explanation:
Concept:
The primary objective of any distribution system is to deliver electrical power to consumers with adequate reliability, acceptable voltage regulation, and minimum interruption. The choice of distribution network depends on factors such as reliability, continuity of supply, cost, and ease of maintenance. The two commonly used distribution systems are:
  • Radial Distribution System
  • Ring Main Distribution System
Radial Distribution System
In a radial distribution system, power flows from the substation to consumers through only one path. \[\text{Substation} \longrightarrow \text{Consumers}\] Characteristics:
  • Simple construction.
  • Lowest installation cost.
  • Easy operation and protection.
  • Entire downstream area loses supply if a feeder fault occurs.
Hence, reliability is comparatively poor. Ring Main Distribution System
In a ring main system, the distributor forms a closed loop connected to the substation. Consumers can receive power from either direction. If a fault develops in one section,
  • only the faulty section is isolated,
  • healthy sections continue receiving supply through the alternate path.
Thus, interruption to consumers is greatly reduced. Analysis of Options
(A) It is less expensive
Incorrect. A ring main system requires additional conductors, switching equipment, and protection devices, making it more expensive than a radial system. (B) Voltage drop in the feeder is less
Although the voltage profile may improve because current is shared through two paths, this is not the principal reason for selecting a ring main system. (C) Power factor is higher
Incorrect. Power factor depends on the nature of the connected load and is independent of the distribution topology. (D) Supply is more reliable
Correct. The ring main system provides an alternative path for power flow, ensuring continuity of supply even when one section is isolated due to maintenance or a fault. Comparison
ParameterRadialRing Main
Initial CostLowHigh
ReliabilityLowHigh
Continuity of SupplyPoorExcellent
Alternative Power PathNoYes
MaintenanceRequires interruptionCan often be performed without interrupting all consumers
Hence, the correct answer is \[\boxed{\text{(D) Supply is more reliable}}\]

questions.question: In a 4-bus system the circuit breakers and the various zones of protection are shown in Figure. If the circuit breakers E, F and G trip, the location of the fault is on .
questions.explanation:
Concept:
A protection zone is a designated part of a power system monitored by a specific set of protective relays and circuit breakers. When a fault occurs within a protection zone, only the circuit breakers surrounding that zone should trip to isolate the faulty section while keeping the healthy portions of the system in service. The overlapping arrangement of protection zones ensures that no part of the power system remains unprotected. --- Analysis of the Given System
The four buses are protected by independent protection zones. For a fault occurring on Bus 2, the breakers that isolate Bus 2 from the rest of the network are \[\boxed{E,\;F,\;\text{and}\;G}\] where
  • Breaker E disconnects Bus 2 from Bus 1.
  • Breaker G disconnects Bus 2 from Bus 3.
  • Breaker F disconnects Bus 2 from Bus 4.
Since all three breakers E, F and G have operated simultaneously, the isolated section is Bus 2. Therefore, the fault must be located on Bus 2. --- Why Other Buses are Incorrect
  • A fault on Bus 1 would require breakers A, B, C and D to operate.
  • A fault on Bus 3 would require breakers H, I and J to trip.
  • A fault on Bus 4 would require breakers K and L to trip.
None of these breaker combinations matches the given condition. --- Hence, the final answer is \[\boxed{\text{Bus 2}}\]

questions.question:
A 50 MVA, 132/66 kV, \(\Delta/Y\), three-phase power transformer is protected by percentage differential relays. The current transformers (CTs) located on the delta and wye sides of the power transformer are 300/5 A and 1200/5 A respectively. Determine
  1. the output current at full load,
  2. the relay current at full load,
  3. the minimum relay current setting to permit 25% overload.
questions.note: No single correct answer in the official key
questions.explanation:
Concept:
Percentage differential protection compares the currents entering and leaving the protected transformer. Under normal operating conditions, after compensating for the transformer ratio and phase shift, the currents supplied to the relay should ideally be equal. Any difference between the compensated CT secondary currents is called the differential (operating) current. --- Step 1: Full-load current on the 66 kV side
The three-phase full-load current is \[I_L=\frac{S}{\sqrt3\,V_L}\] Substituting, \[I_L = \frac{50\times10^6} {\sqrt3\times66\times10^3}\] \[\boxed{I_L=437.39~\text{A}}\] --- Step 2: Current supplied by the delta-side CT
The CT ratio is \[300/5=60:1\] The line current corresponding to the relay is \[I_1 = 437.39 \left( \frac{66/\sqrt3}{132} \right) = 126.26~\text{A}\] Hence, the CT secondary current is \[I_{CT1} = \frac{126.26}{60} = 2.104~\text{A}\] --- Step 3: Current supplied by the wye-side CT
The CT ratio is \[1200/5=240:1\] Therefore, \[I_{CT2} = \frac{437.39}{240} = 1.822~\text{A}\] --- Step 4: Differential (relay) current
The relay operating current is the difference between the compensated CT secondary currents. \[I_{\text{relay}} = I_{CT1}-I_{CT2}\] \[= 2.104-1.822\] \[\boxed{I_{\text{relay}}=0.2815~\text{A}}\] --- Step 5: Relay current setting for 25% overload
The restraining (through) current is \[I_{\text{through}} = \frac{I_{CT1}+I_{CT2}}{2}\] \[= \frac{2.104+1.822}{2} = 1.963~\text{A}\] To permit a 25% overload, \[1.25\,I_{\text{relay}} = (\text{Current Setting}) \times I_{\text{through}}\] Hence, \[\text{Current Setting} = \frac{1.25\times0.2815}{1.963}\] \[= 0.1792\] Therefore, \[\boxed{\text{Current Setting}=17.92\%}\] --- Thus, the final answer is \[\boxed{ \begin{aligned} (a)\;&437.39~\text{A}\\ (b)\;&0.2815~\text{A}\\ (c)\;&17.92\% \end{aligned} }\]

Operating states of a diode:
